description: Somos un grupo de estudiantes de sexto grado creativos y con inquitud por el desarrollo de la ciencia y la tecnologia.
summary: Sound Of The EARTH is a free, accessible web app that turns NASA Earth data into real-time spatial sound. From the cockpit of a "spaceship," users choose a mission (sea surface temperature, vegetation, rainfall, or true-color imagery from NASA GIBS, plus datasets from the Earth Information Center's VEDA catalog) and listen as the ship sweeps the planet from west to east: higher values play higher notes, missing data is silence, and west-to-east is panned left-to-right. Active wildfires, storms, volcanoes, and sea ice from NASA EONET play their own sound effects as they are crossed. A built-in game, "¿Dónde suena?" (Where does it sound?), asks players to compare two real places by ear alone. The app works with keyboard only and includes voice narration and spoken map descriptions. It answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge by pairing EIC visuals with live sonification, so that blind and low-vision people, and children who learn by listening, can explore our changing planet. Created by team StudiosIA Lab (6th graders, Barranquilla, Colombia); AI-assisted coding declared.
details:
What is it, and how does it work? *Sound of the Earth* is a web-based "spaceship" that includes a video game mode; it converts NASA data into spatial sound in real time, allowing you to "hear" the planet. The "Explore" tab features four missions—covering sea temperature, vegetation and forests, rainfall, and real-world imagery—all sourced from NASA GIBS, plus an additional mission connected to the Earth Information Center (VEDA) data catalog. When you press "Listen" (▶), the spaceship travels around the globe from west to east: higher data values ​​produce higher-pitched notes, while an absence of data results in silence. Sounds from the west play through the left speaker, and those from the east through the right. Active events such as fires, storms, volcanoes, and ice (via NASA EONET) are represented by unique sound effects. In the "Video Game" tab, the game "Where Is It Sounding?" presents two real-world locations—one in each ear—and challenges the player to guess which one is hotter, greener, or rainier, with a system of points, lives, and medals.

What are the benefits? It makes Earth science accessible to children, people who are blind or have low vision, and those who learn best by listening. It can be operated using only a keyboard, features a voice narrator, and includes a button that provides a verbal description of the map. A mini-game teaches users how to "read" data by ear through play. It is free and runs in any web browser, requiring no installation.

What is the intended impact? To enable schools, museums, and individuals with visual impairments to explore the planet using real-time data, helping them understand what it is like and how it changes. If children learn to "listen" to the Earth, they will grow up wanting to take care of it. Any new data from the EIC can be made audible without needing to modify the code.

What tools did we use? HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single file. The Web Audio API for spatial sound (echo and stereo), the Canvas API to read colors from images, the `fetch` API to retrieve data, and the Speech Synthesis API for the narrator. Data sources: NASA GIBS, NASA EONET, and the Earth Information Center’s VEDA catalog. Published using GitHub and Netlify, with Google Drive as a resource. No special hardware was required. The concept and the solution were developed by the team; the programming was carried out with the assistance of a superintelligence (Claude, by Anthropic) using the "vibe coding" methodology.

In what sense is it creative? It places children in the cockpit of a spacecraft—where every piece of data becomes a mission—and incorporates a video game that can be played with one’s eyes closed. The sound design is spatial: the world unfolds from left to right, as if the user were flying over it, with each natural phenomenon assigned its own distinct sound (fire crackles, a storm roars with wind, a volcano resonates like a drum). We use a pentatonic scale to ensure the data always sounds harmonious, while the mini-game transforms data comparison into an engaging challenge for children.

What factors did the team take into account? Accessibility (keyboard, voice, contrast, and screen readers), the use of real, up-to-date NASA data, scientific integrity (we clarify that the values ​​are derived from colors and are therefore approximations), ensuring the experience is fun for children, making it free to use on any device, and being transparent about the use of AI.

Team and process: StudiosIA Lab—five sixth-grade students from Colegio Cristiano El Salvador (Barranquilla, Colombia): Dominick Rozas León, Emiliano García González, Esteban Gómez Alonso, Matias Mancera Crespo, and Derek Manes Contreras—with their lead mentor, Orietta Bueno Maldonado.

Website: https://latierraseescucha.netlify.app · Code: 'la-tierra-se-escucha' repository on GitHub
dataRefs: NASA EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker)
